payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Put a frog in the toilet
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Add a frog inside the toilet.
node.criteria: Use only the saved support observations. Return complete when s1 passes; s2 may then be skipped and is unnecessary for completion. When s1 fails, return partial if s2 establishes requested progress, absent if s2 establishes no requested progress, and unknown if s2 is unknown or unexpectedly skipped. When s1 is unknown, return partial only if s2's evidence establishes requested progress short of completion; return absent only if its evidence explicitly establishes no requested progress, including no completed placement. Otherwise return unknown: failure to find an incomplete placement attempt does not itself resolve uncertain completion. A skipped support is unobserved, not a failure. Extra frogs outside the bowl neither establish requested progress by themselves nor negate a genuine placement inside it. Do not add requirements for frog count, realism, removal of extra frogs, or alteration of pre-existing bowl details.
node.binding: Target: A frog is visibly placed within the toilet bowl.. Reference: The toilet in the input image..

node_traces.evidence: s1 passes: a frog is visibly situated inside the toilet bowl. Under the saved criteria, s2 is unnecessary for completion.

dependencies.evidence: A frog is visibly situated inside the toilet bowl, below the rim and within the bowl opening. Other frogs on the lid and nearby floor do not negate this placement.

response.content: {"text":"The node’s binding is truncated/underspecified (“A frog (...) frog inside the toilet”) and omits the reference toilet, while the executable criteria appear to treat one positive observation as sufficient completion. In the edited image, a frog is clearly inside the bowl, but additional frogs are on the lid, tank area, and floor; the source has no frogs. The reference label “partial” therefore conflicts with the trace’s “complete/yes,” but it does not establish which individual placement is required. Repair the binding and criterion mapping so the node evaluates the requested change against the source/reference and preserves the rubric’s distinction between partial and complete, without inferring that extra frogs negate a valid bowl placement. Check whether the saved support observations and their routing actually represent all relevant requested progress; do not treat s2’s conditional skip as negative evidence or as proof that completion is warranted. The trace’s high confidence is not a resolution of the criterion ambiguity. Keep transport/schema issues separate: the trace is valid and queried, and the skipped dependency is explicitly conditional, so this is a semantic/routing diagnosis rather than an observation failure."}
